segments.content:
Chapter 120: 0117 Peking University Professors Play Legends of the Three Kingdoms Too?

The Veritable Records of the Ming Dynasty totals about 16 million characters. The work of proofreading, punctuating, and organizing it is extremely tedious, not something one or two scholars could complete.

Over in Taiwan, they created a photolithographic copy of the red-lined edition of the Veritable Records of the Ming Dynasty in 1962.

Peking University obtained the Taiwanese photolithographic copy in 1963 and used it as the base text, collating it with various other editions for proofreading and supplementation.

But the work was interrupted during a certain period.

After 1977, the project was restarted. Due to various reasons, the project team members changed significantly, and it was no longer clear just how many people had participated.

This version from Peking University, compared to the Taiwanese photolithographic copy, corrected over ten thousand historical errors and omissions and also included supplementary historical materials like the Veritable Records of Chongzhen and the Chongzhen Longbian.

After all, the scope of the project was too massive, and there were still omissions. Every now and then, someone would find another one.

Chen Guilang parked his bicycle in front of the teaching building and was chatting idly with a classmate.

As they chatted, Chen Guilang said, "Sorry, I need to go ask the professor a question."

"See you later, then."

"See you."

Waving goodbye, Chen Guilang walked over quickly and intercepted Professor Wang, who had just finished class. "Hello, Professor Wang. May I ask you a question?"

Professor Wang was sixty years old this year, an expert in Ming and Qing history, and one of the instructors for the Yuanpei Program's exclusive course, History of Chinese Civilization.

He carried a briefcase and adjusted his glasses. "Talk as we walk."

Chen Guilang immediately went to get his bicycle, jogging to catch up. "Professor Wang, regarding the records of Emperor Yingzong's restoration, why are there discrepancies between the History of Ming and the Veritable Records of the Ming Dynasty?"

Professor Wang stopped and sized up Chen Guilang seriously. "Are you a graduate student in the history department?"

"I'm a freshman in the Yuanpei Program. You'll be teaching us next semester," Chen Guilang said, taking the opportunity to build a connection.

Professor Wang seemed slightly surprised. "A freshman is already reading the Veritable Records of the Ming Dynasty?"

Chen Guilang said, "I'm writing a popular history novel about the Ming Dynasty. It's not even at an introductory level; it's written specifically for readers unfamiliar with Ming history. I hope to get more people interested in and knowledgeable about the Ming Dynasty, and in turn, attract them to study it."

"That's a very good idea," Professor Wang said. "The public really doesn't pay much attention to the Ming Dynasty. Its popularity is far less than that of the Song and Qing."

In 2004, the Ming Dynasty's popularity online hadn't taken off yet.

Chen Guilang said, "While I was writing, I noticed some inconsistencies between the History of Ming and the Veritable Records of the Ming Dynasty. Especially recently, when I was researching Emperor Yingzong's Duomen Coup."

Professor Wang continued walking forward and said with a smile, "The History of Ming's account of Emperor Yingzong's restoration discarded the Veritable Records and cited unofficial histories instead. That's why they don't match up."

"Why would they use unofficial histories instead of the official one?" Chen Guilang asked, appearing very eager to learn.

Professor Wang explained, "Because the Veritable Records of Emperor Yingzong of Ming was fabricated, and very obviously so."

"To cover for the emperor's reputation?" Chen Guilang asked.

Professor Wang nodded. "The scholars who compiled the Veritable Records of Emperor Yingzong of Ming were, on one hand, concealing his faults, while on the other, leaving behind clues. These clues happened to align with several unofficial histories, and they also align with other biographies in the History of Ming. Therefore, when the History of Ming was compiled during the Qing Dynasty, this section was carefully scrutinized. Emperor Yingzong's restoration must have been a military coup."

Chen Guilang asked, "Then did the Jingtai Emperor die of illness, or was he murdered?"

"It's questionable," Professor Wang said. "The Veritable Records of Emperor Yingzong of Ming uses a lot of euphemistic language regarding the Jingtai Emperor's death. The more they try to cover it up, the more suspicious the truth becomes. Some unofficial histories say he was strangled, but that's an isolated claim. It's hard to verify now, so we can only say it's questionable, with a high probability of it not being a natural death."

"Thank you for clearing up my confusion, Professor Wang," Chen Guilang said respectfully.

Professor Wang was quite pleased. "It's rare for young people to be interested in studying history. And for you to start reading the Veritable Records of the Ming Dynasty as a freshman is even rarer. You Yuanpei Program students can choose your courses freely, so you should take more of my classes next time. If you have any questions in the future, feel free to come find me anytime."

Chen Guilang took out a printed manuscript of the first thirty thousand words of Those Things in the Ming Dynasty. "This is the simple popular history book I'm writing. I'd like to ask you for your critiques, Professor Wang."

Professor Wang took the manuscript and began reading as he walked. "Heh, your writing style is quite interesting."

Chen Guilang said, "I posted it on the Peking University BBS, and students from the history department called it a children's book."

"It is written in a very simple and plain style," Professor Wang said. "Has anyone criticized you for any factual errors?"

Chen Guilang said, "Not for that. But some history students have criticized my evaluations of historical events as being too one-sided and shallow."

Professor Wang chuckled. "That means you've written it very successfully; they can't find any real faults. Your book is an introduction to popular history, so of course it can't be written too profoundly. Even professional historians, when giving lectures to ordinary students, will deliberately speak in very simple terms, because if they don't, no one will listen."

"You flatter me, Professor Wang," Chen Guilang said.

Professor Wang asked, "How many words have you written?"

Chen Guilang said, "About three hundred thousand. I plan to write over a million words."

Professor Wang said, "I can help you contact Peking University Press. Peking University publishes a lot of academic monographs, but introductory books like yours that respect official history are relatively rare. I think it's worth promoting. When it's published, I can write the foreword for you."

He hadn't even asked, and the professor was already offering to write a foreword?

Chen Guilang said, "Thank you for your high regard, Professor Wang, but a publisher has already taken an interest in this book."

"Which publisher?" Professor Wang asked.

Chen Guilang said, "A newly established publishing company. They're very sincere, offering a tiered royalty rate with a guaranteed 15%. If it sells well, the royalties could go as high as 20%."

"20%? You haven't run into a scammer, have you?" Professor Wang said in surprise.

Even when he published his own books, the royalty rate never exceeded 10%. Because the sales of academic monographs are limited...

Chen Guilang said, "He's not a scammer. The man used to be a famous author and a shareholder in a literary website. After the website was acquired, he cashed out his shares and went into publishing. This person is very good at generating hype. My book isn't even finished, and he's already built up buzz for me in the newspapers and online."

Professor Wang smiled. "Then you're quite lucky, to run into someone so generous right when you start writing. You didn't just come looking for me today to have me write a foreword, did you?"

"My main purpose was to ask you for guidance," Chen Guilang didn't deny it.

Professor Wang wasn't angry either. "Although I have some small fame in academic circles, ordinary readers have probably never heard of an old relic like me. A foreword from me won't do much to boost your sales."

Seeing how easygoing he was, Chen Guilang decided to joke, half-truthfully, "It's written so simply that I'm afraid people will criticize me. I was hoping you could lend me your name for some credibility."

"So I'm just a shield," Professor Wang laughed. "Come on, I'll help you find another shield. That professor has also pivoted to popularizing history in the last couple of years. He'll definitely love your book. Like me, he's a vice-chairman of the Chinese Society for Ming Dynasty Studies. Although he's not from our university, he often comes to Peking University to give lectures on Ming history."

Professor Wang took out his phone and made a call. "Old Shang, are you done with your lecture? Good, I'm heading over to find you."

Hearing "Old Shang," Chen Guilang already guessed who it was. The man would later go on to talk about the Yongle Emperor on the program Lecture Room.

Some critics described him as: sufficient in popularization, lacking in innovation.

But Professor Shang began receiving a national stipend in his forties.

Chen Guilang continued to ask Professor Wang historical questions. Some he genuinely didn't understand, others he pretended not to. In any case, asking was all that mattered. It was right up Professor Wang's alley; he liked it when students sought his guidance.

Professor Shang was very close with Professor Wang. They had once proofread the Veritable Records of the Ming Dynasty together at Peking University, and he was frequently invited to lecture there.

"Old Wang, you've taken on a new student?" Professor Shang glanced at Chen Guilang.

Professor Wang laughed. "A freshman. Came to ask me about the Veritable Records of the Ming Dynasty. He was asking why the accounts of Emperor Yingzong's restoration in the History of Ming and the Veritable Records have discrepancies."

"That's rare for a freshman. Looks like a promising one," Professor Shang asked. "What's your name?"

Chen Guilang bowed. "Hello, Professor Shang. My name is Chen Guilang."

Professor Shang smiled too. "You're the one who wrote Those Things in the Ming Dynasty on the Tianya forum, right?"

"Professor Shang uses Tianya too?" Chen Guilang feigned surprise.

This reaction was very pleasing to Professor Shang. "You think I'm an old fossil? I'm a veteran netizen; I started going online years ago. Not only do I know you're writing Those Things in the Ming Dynasty, I also know you started a 'Campus Belle' contest on Xiaonei."

Chen Guilang looked embarrassed. "I'm ashamed."

Professor Shang questioned, "Why does Xiaonei only allow students to register? I'm a teacher, and when I tried to register, it insisted I select a department and class."

"Well... that's a feature that's still under development," Chen Guilang answered vaguely.

Professor Wang asked, "What's this Xiaonei 'Campus Belle' contest?"

Professor Shang pointed at Chen Guilang. "This student created a website that lets students vote for their own department and campus belles. The activity has even spread to our university."

Professor Wang found it novel. "You young people really have active minds. We didn't have these kinds of opportunities back in our day."

"We had class, department, and campus belles back then too, but it was all just unofficial gossip. We'd never dare to talk about it openly," Professor Shang said.

Professor Shang sat in front of the computer and entered Xiaonei as a guest. He said to Professor Wang, "Come take a look. This is the Xiaonei he made... whoa, nine universities are already holding campus belle contests. Your website is quite influential."

Professor Wang leaned over curiously and watched with great interest.

Chen Guilang complained inwardly, *Aren't you two getting off topic?*

Professor Shang said, "A student of mine told me this website has many other features, like creating and joining groups. There's even a history interest group where students can discuss historical questions online. Uh... Xiao Chen, come over and give us a demonstration."

Chen Guilang could only log into his own account and apply to join a history interest group.

Professor Wang sat and watched the computer screen for a long time before saying with approval, "This is great. Students from different years and different departments, as long as they love history, can discuss it together without even leaving their rooms."

Professor Shang asked, "So, when will Xiaonei allow teachers to register?"

"I'll have the programmers work on it as soon as I get back."

Seeing their interest in the internet, Chen Guilang simply switched the topic to Legends of the Three Kingdoms. "I also made a history-themed game. It just went online two days ago. Would you two professors like to give it a try?"

Professor Wang wasn't interested in games.

But Professor Shang said, "Download it and let's have a look."

Legends of the Three Kingdoms didn't have a web version yet; you had to download the client.

The internet speed here was quite fast. While Professor Shang chatted idly and read the manuscript, Legends of the Three Kingdoms finished downloading in no time.

"There's a new player tutorial..." Chen Guilang reminded him.

Professor Shang registered his game name as "Yongle Emperor." It seemed he really did like Zhu Di.

After finishing the tutorial, Professor Shang eagerly entered an eight-player game. Professor Wang, sitting beside him, was surprisingly engrossed in watching.

It looked like these two were about to get hooked!

Sure enough, after watching a few rounds, Professor Wang said to Chen Guilang, "Go to my office in a bit and help me download the game. I don't know how."

Chen Guilang: "Okay..."

(End of this chapter)
